comparedAgainst: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/async-scenarios — Microsoft Learn's own async-programming overview, fetched in full. It warns in one paragraph that 'synchronous blocking on asynchronous operations can lead to deadlocks and should be avoided whenever possible' and never once reproduces a deadlock — no code, no repro, no detection technique. It does give the async-void bullet list this article quotes verbatim ('exceptions thrown in an async void method can't be caught outside of that method', 'difficult to test', 'negative side effects'), confirmed exact.

Confirms the state-machine field names (`<>1__state`, `<>t__builder`), the 'no allocation unless the method actually suspends' claim, ExecutionContext flow, AwaitOnCompleted vs AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted — and, importantly, contains the exact fact the article's hardest empirical claim rests on: 'in debug builds the C# compiler will actually generate these state machine types as classes, as doing so can aid in certain debugging exercises.' This independently corroborates the article's own 64 B (debug) → 0 B (Optimize=true) measurement from a completely different source than the one the article cites for it.

justification:
Ran `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/csharp-dotnet/async-await.md` from PowerShell five times (not the requested 3-4, to be safe given the concurrency content): PASS, blocks=36, executed=19, byte-identical result every time, no flakiness. I then went further than the harness on the three most timing-sensitive demos, using my own standalone `dotnet run` harness in Git Bash: the deadlock block run 5 independent times (always 'still blocked after 2000 ms: this is the deadlock', wall time ~2.4 s each — the 200 ms operation never sneaks in under the 2000 ms detection window, a 10x margin with zero variance); the ConfigureAwait(false) fix run 5 independent times (always 'result: 42' / 'finished before the timeout: no deadlock', wall time ~0.6 s each); and the WhenAll exception-aggregation block run 6 independent times (always 'second failed' then 'first failed', in that exact order, matching the article's shown output exactly). Eleven additional standalone runs beyond the five full-article runs, sixteen executions total across the load-bearing concurrency blocks, zero deviation.

**Independent verdict on the deadlock: it is genuinely, structurally real — not staged, not accidentally avoided.** I traced the cycle by hand against the actual code rather than trusting the prose: (1) `ExclusiveContext` is a sound minimal analogue of WindowsFormsSynchronizationContext/DispatcherSynchronizationContext — Cleary's own table (which I fetched) describes both as 'Specific Thread Used to Execute Delegates: Yes' and 'Exclusive (Delegates Execute One at a Time): Yes', and `ExclusiveContext.Post` only enqueues onto a `BlockingCollection` that one dedicated background thread drains one item at a time via `GetConsumingEnumerable`, which is exactly that shape; real WinForms/WPF Post is also documented as never invoking the delegate directly ('Post May Invoke Delegate Directly: Never'), matching this implementation's always-enqueue behavior. (2) The circular wait is real, not simulated: `SetSynchronizationContext(pump)` runs on the pump thread itself, so `SynchronizationContext.Current` really is `pump` when `FetchAsync`'s `await Task.Delay(200)` captures it (per the state-machine mechanics demonstrated earlier in the same article); `.Result` genuinely blocks that same pump thread; 200 ms later the timer's continuation is handed to `pump.Post`, which only enqueues — the one thread that could ever dequeue and run it is parked inside `.Result`. Neither side can make progress; this is a textbook circular wait, reconstructed from first principles, not asserted. (3) `ManualResetEventSlim.Wait(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2))` is a sound way to prove a permanent deadlock without hanging the harness: the genuine work only needs 200 ms, so 2000 ms is a 10x margin, and because the pump thread is `IsBackground = true`, the process can still exit cleanly even though that thread is deadlocked forever — the timeout only bounds the *test*, not the deadlocked thread, which is the right design. (4) The `ConfigureAwait(false)` fix genuinely resolves it rather than dodging it: it stops `AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted` from capturing `pump` in the first place, so the delay's continuation is posted to the thread pool instead, completing the `Task` from a thread nobody is blocking on; `.Result` on the pump thread still blocks for the real 200 ms (verified: ~0.6 s wall time for the whole test, not near-zero) but is woken by an internal completion signal that has nothing to do with `pump`'s queue. I did not find any way this demo could pass by accident (e.g. a race letting the continuation slip in before `.Result` starts waiting) — the 2-second margin and 5-for-5/6-for-6 reproducibility rule that out.

**Sourcing checked against primary text, not summaries.** Every quoted fragment I checked against the fetched page came back verbatim: the `await` operator page ('suspends evaluation of the enclosing async method... doesn't block the thread... control returns to the caller'), the TAP overview ('doesn't force a method to run asynchronously on another thread. It enables await, and the method runs synchronously until it reaches an incomplete awaitable'), the SynchronizationContext class page ('a free-threaded context with no synchronization'), the 2011 MSDN Magazine piece (WinForms/WPF 'executed one at a time... by a specific UI thread, in the order they were queued'; classic ASP.NET '[will ]ensure that they execute one at a time'; console apps/services 'by default, all threads... only have the default SynchronizationContext' — all three confirmed against the fetched archive page), the ConfigureAwait FAQ ('by specifying false, even if there is a current context or scheduler to call back to, it pretends as if there isn't'), Task.WhenAll's Remarks (the Faulted/aggregation sentence, exact), the ValueTask docs (both the 'default choice... should be Task' sentence and the three-item 'never do this' list, exact), and the async-scenarios page's three async-void bullets, exact. I also independently corroborated the article's hardest claim — the 64 B (debug) → 0 B (`Optimize=true`) ValueTask finding — against Toub's devblog post, which states outright that debug builds compile async state machines as classes rather than structs specifically to aid debugging; that is precisely the mechanism the article's finding requires (a class-based state machine allocates on construction regardless of whether the method ever actually suspends, while a struct-based one only boxes if it suspends), and it is a genuinely non-obvious, well-differentiated finding — most ValueTask coverage stops at 'it avoids allocation,' full stop.

Two things keep this off a 9.5+, neither a factual error. First, `docs/EDITORIAL_BRIEF.md`'s binding pilot lesson is explicit that an uncited source in the front-matter list is a finding: 'Foreground and background threads' (learn.microsoft.com/.../foreground-and-background-threads) is listed in `sources` but never linked or discussed anywhere in the body, even though `IsBackground = true` appears twice in the deadlock/fix code — the natural place to use it. Second, the three ValueTask measurement blocks (72 B, 0 B, 64 B, 0 B) are pinned to exact, un-wildcarded byte counts from `GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread()`; unlike the article's timing lines (correctly wildcarded with `[...]`), these numbers are a function of this specific .NET 10.0.401 x64 build's object layout (header size, `Task<T>`'s field layout, the debug-mode state-machine class's field layout) rather than of machine load, so they are far more reproducible than a timing — I confirmed this empirically by getting the same three numbers on all five full-article runs — but a future servicing release that changes any of those object layouts by even one field would fail these three blocks and nothing else, the same category of shell-fragility the unit-testing-fundamentals round-1 review flagged for xUnit's frame-count-sensitive stack traces. Both are real findings; neither is a wrong or misleading claim, and I found no factual error anywhere in the article after checking every non-trivial claim against a fetched primary source or my own independent runs.
